330.title: The first mountain, from the top
330.word: the whole year in one sit
330.hook: you've been climbing for 329 days: today, turn around and look down the trail
330.howItsDone: Many Hindus mark the end of a period of study or a vow with a pause to look back, often with a puja or a visit to a teacher to give thanks; people who finish reading the whole Gita sometimes celebrate its completion.

segments.voice: Last week, the guided visits, under one strand name: what a Buddhist means by the breath. Six houses heard in their own words, and then namaste came home. Did you see one person as more than a person? Day three hundred thirty.

Anyone who has climbed a real hill knows this moment. You've been staring at your feet for hours: the next rock, the next root, the next switchback. Your legs hurt. You haven't looked up in a long time. And then the trail flattens, and there's nowhere higher to step, and you turn around. And the whole path is lying there below you, the parking lot tiny, the first bend you thought was steep looking like nothing at all. You did that. One step a day. Today there's no new idea. Today we turn around.
screen: `EYES ON YOUR FEET FOR MONTHS.` → `THE TRAIL FLATTENS.` → `TURN AROUND.`

segments.voice: Look down the trail. At the very bottom, camp one: twenty-one words. Namaste, om, dharma, shanti, karma, atman, Brahman, seva, bhakti, moksha, and the rest. Words you'd said for years without knowing, and words you'd never heard. You learned that you already spoke some Sanskrit. A little higher, camp two: the stories. Ganesha and his broken tusk. Hanuman's leap. The whole Ramayana as a serial, Rama and Sita and the long road home. Then the Mahabharata's cliffhangers, leaving two armies on a field. Higher still, camp three: the practices. Breath, mantra, a small shrine, a flame at sunset, food as offering, the temple, the festivals. The path stopped being something you listened to and became something you did. Then the steep part, camp four: the Bhagavad Gita, all eighteen chapters, about seven hundred verses, read in order. Arjuna dropping his bow. Krishna's answer. Chapter eleven's terrifying vision. And at the end, the line where Krishna hands the choice back to Arjuna: do as you choose. You read the whole thing. And the last stretch, camp five: the depths. The Upanishads, Isha, Kena, Katha, Mandukya. The three paths of action, devotion and knowledge. Advaita and Dvaita side by side, never ranked. The Yoga Sutras' first line: now, yoga. A track of your own choosing. And last week, a guest in six other houses. That's the first mountain. Not the whole range; the first mountain. The Hindu tradition would say you haven't finished anything. You've just learned to walk. But from up here, the steps add up.
screen: `CAMP ONE: TWENTY-ONE WORDS.` · `CAMPS TWO AND THREE: STORIES, PRACTICES.` · `CAMP FOUR: THE WHOLE GITA.` · `CAMP FIVE: THE DEPTHS.` · then, large: `LOOK HOW FAR.`

segments.voice: The whole year in one sit. Close your eyes. Breathe in, and remember a word from camp one, any word. Breathe out. Breathe in, and remember a story: a monkey, a bridge, a chariot. Breathe out. Breathe in, and remember something you did: a flame, a mantra, a meal. Breathe out. Breathe in, and remember one line from the Gita that stayed. Breathe out. Breathe in, and remember one question from the depths: who am I? Then just rest at the top. The bell holds the time.
The whole year in one sit. Twenty-one words, the stories, the practices, the whole Gita and the depths, held for two minutes at once, the way a view holds a trail.
screen: `THE WHOLE YEAR IN ONE SIT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: look how far. Today, tell one person one thing you know now that you didn't know a year ago. Just one. Day three hundred thirty.

match.prompt: each camp and what it held — tap the pairs.

reaching the top of year one means the path is finished
it's the first mountain, not the whole range: from here, the ranges begin.
this year taught Advaita as the right answer and Dvaita as the wrong one
they were taught side by side as electives, never ranked.

fork.setup: you've reached the top of a long climb. what's the first thing to do?
options: start up the next peak immediately.
turn around and look how far you came.
check how many steps other people took.
fork.reveal: today is for turning around. no new idea: just the view, and the steps adding up.

original.note: Sanskrit śikhara: a mountain peak, and also the name for the tall tower over a north Indian temple's shrine.

trapdoor: what you thought: the summit is the end of the climb.
what it means: the top of the first mountain: a place to turn around and see the whole trail at once.
what a scholar hears: the shikhara, peak, over a north Indian temple's inner shrine is built to echo a mountain, often read as Meru or Kailash.

331.title: Year one close
331.hook: from the top of the first mountain, you can see the next ones: the Upanishads, the Ramayana, the Yoga Sutras, your track
331.howItsDone: Hindu study is traditionally lifelong: people return to the Upanishads, the epics and the Gita again and again, often with a teacher, and many families hear the Ramayana or the Bhagavata Purana recited over days or weeks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the whole year in one sit. Words, stories, practices, the Gita, the depths, all held at once. Your line was look how far. Did you tell someone one thing you know now? Day three hundred thirty-one.

There's a second thing that happens at the top of a mountain, a minute after the first. You've turned around and looked at the trail. You've caught your breath. And then you turn back the other way, and you see it. Behind this peak, there's another. And behind that one, a whole line of them, blue and white and going on past where your eyes can follow. The first mountain was the one you could see from the parking lot. The ranges were hiding behind it the whole time. This is the last day of year one. Today we look at what's ahead.
screen: `THE SECOND MINUTE AT THE TOP.` → `ANOTHER PEAK, THEN ANOTHER.` → `THE LAST DAY OF YEAR ONE.`

segments.voice: Start with where you stand. Year one gave you the vocabulary, the stories, the practices, one complete scripture read in order, and a first look at the depths. That's a real thing. Many people meet the Gita through its best-loved verses; reading it straight through, in order, is a real undertaking. Now look ahead. The first range is the rest of the principal Upanishads. You met four of them this year. Year two opens the others, beginning tomorrow with the Chandogya, one of the oldest and longest, and its teaching on om, which it calls the essence of essences. Later in that range you'll reach the lines Hindus have quoted for well over two thousand years, like the Chandogya's tat tvam asi: you are that. The second range is the Ramayana again, but this time as a year-long serial, the full story, slowly, the way families once heard it over many evenings. The third is the Yoga Sutras complete: all one hundred ninety-five short threads of Patanjali, not just the opening. Then your lineage track in full, whichever you walked. And behind those, farther off: the Mahabharata as a serial, the Puranas, the saints and poets from the Alvars to Kabir to Vivekananda. Nobody climbs all of that in a week. The Hindu tradition has never pretended you would. The Katha Upanishad, which you read this year, tells the seeker to arise, awake, and learn from those who know, and it says the path is as sharp as a razor's edge and hard to cross. It never says the path is short. That's not a warning. It's an invitation. There's more. There's always more.
screen: `WHERE YOU STAND: THE FIRST MOUNTAIN.` · `THE REST OF THE UPANISHADS.` · `THE RAMAYANA, THE YOGA SUTRAS, YOUR TRACK.` · `ARISE, AWAKE: THE PATH IS LONG.` · then, large: `THE RANGES AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Last sit of year one. Sit tall, like someone at the top of a hill. Breathe in, and feel what you carry now that you didn't carry a year ago: a word, a story, a habit, a question. Breathe out, and let it settle. Then turn, in your mind, toward the ranges. You don't have to know how you'll climb them. Just see them there, waiting, patient as mountains are. If you pray, you can bring your own thanks for the year. The bell holds the time.
The ranges ahead. The rest of the Upanishads, the Ramayana as a serial, the Yoga Sutras complete, your lineage track in full, and farther peaks behind them. The first mountain was only the first.
Your line: there's more. There's always more. Today, before you sleep, name one thing from this year you want to understand better next year. That's day three hundred thirty-one, and year one.

match.prompt: the ranges ahead — tap the pairs.

the Katha Upanishad calls the path as sharp as a razor's edge

the Yoga Sutras have one hundred ninety-five sutras in the common count
year one read the opening; the ranges read all of them.

fork.setup: you've reached the top of the first mountain and seen the ranges behind it. what do you do tomorrow?
options: take one more small step, the way you took every other.
try to climb every range at once.
fork.reveal: the whole year was one step a day. the ranges are climbed the same way, starting tomorrow with the Chandogya.

original.note: Sanskrit himālaya: hima, snow, + ālaya, abode: the abode of snow, the great range.

trapdoor: what you thought: year one is the course, and now it's over.
what it means: year one is the first mountain; the ranges, the rest of the texts, start tomorrow.
what a scholar hears: the Katha's arise, awake (1.3.14) became a watchword of Swami Vivekananda, who made it a call to a whole generation.
